body: Lights first, then the radio, because the radio takes a moment to come round. A woman has just unlocked the hairdressing shop, half past eight on a Tuesday, on a parade of five with two of them empty. What arrives is a quarter of the way through a song she does not know. She sweeps up the bit of yesterday the brush missed, fills the kettle, writes two names on the board for eleven and half past twelve, and the song finishes somewhere behind her without her having properly heard the end of it. She does not go back for it.
That is the whole difference between a broadcast and a library, in the order of two switches. She did not choose a track. She joined something that was already going on.

46 of the 121 assigned frequencies on this band are live and playing at this moment. The rest are named, described and in build. A frequency is reserved before a station is finished, the same way a broadcaster holds a licence.

It is worth being exact about what live means here, because the word has been worn thin by people using it to mean available. A station is on air when it is playing whether or not anybody is listening to it. There is a position in the hour that you did not set and cannot move, and it goes on advancing while you are asleep, while the tab is closed, while you are arguing about something in another room. Nothing is waiting for you to arrive. Two people who tune to the same number at the same second get the same song, which sounds trivial and is the property everything else on this band is built on.

The ones playing right now are these: Year of Jubilee, Torah Sings, The Upper Room, Celebrate Yeshua!, Yes and Amen, God's Little Lambs, Jubilee Kids Party, Bucky's Barnyard, Gospel Country, Pentecostal Shout, Riddim and Rhyme, The Ancient Paths, Corner Cipher, Throne Room Vegas, Gravel Road Gospel, Gospel By Music, Radiant Stones Concerts, Midnight Praise, Island Hallelujah, Familia Inspire (Español), Brasil Inspire (Português), Asia Inspire (中文), Inspire India (हिन्दी), Inspire Crown (العربية), France Inspire (Français), Jubilee Praise (Română), Deutschland Inspire (Deutsch), Russia Inspire (Русский), Italia Inspire (Italiano), Pilipinas Inspire (Tagalog), Vietnam Inspire (Tiếng Việt), Polska Inspire (Polski), Portugal Inspire (Português), Nederland Inspire (Nederlands), Danmark Inspire (Dansk), Sverige Inspire (Svenska), Česko Inspire (Čeština), Magyar Inspire (Magyar), Bulgaria Inspire (Български), Türkiye Inspire (Türkçe), Israel Inspire (עברית), Thailand Inspire (ไทย), Japan Inspire (日本語), Melody’s Sparkle, Latin Worship (English-Spanish), Hebraic Celebrations. Every one of them holds a single permanent frequency between HM 300.30 and HM 398.70, and no two share a number.

What reaches the air is governed by a rule that costs a good deal to keep. Every live station plays from a published manifest: nothing goes out that is not in the catalogue, and every track carries a permanent twelve-character SongID that the rotation and the play logs know it by. That is an ordinary discipline for a broadcaster and a rare one for a streaming service. It means nothing can be slipped in at the last minute, nothing can be swapped for a similar recording, and anything that plays can be traced afterwards to the file it came from and the passage it stands on.

Almost nothing else people listen to works this way any more. The ordinary experience of a music service is that you cannot find out what it played you last Tuesday, that a track you liked has quietly left the catalogue with no notice given, and that the thing described as a station is in fact a private sequence assembled for you and discarded afterwards. Nobody is being deceived exactly. There is simply nothing there to check, and after a while people stop expecting there to be, which is the more serious loss of the two.

The same identifier is why a song can sit on several frequencies at once without anybody losing track of what it is. A worship track can be in rotation on the flagship, on a Spanish-language frequency and on a hymn station in the same afternoon, and it is the same file with the same credits and the same Scripture attached in all three places. That overlap is intended rather than accidental. A broadcast band is not a set of walled catalogues; it is one catalogue seen from several angles.
There is a serious alternative to all of this and it is worth stating fairly.

It is the personalised stream, and it does one thing better than any broadcaster ever has: it fits. It learns what you skip, it stops playing what you hate, and it never makes you sit through four minutes of something that was clearly meant for somebody else. Millions of hours of genuine enjoyment come out of it every day and it would be silly to pretend otherwise. But it cannot be broadcast, and that is not a small technicality. Nothing can be published in advance, because nothing exists in advance. Nobody else is hearing it. And the question of what was on at four o’clock has no answer at all, because there was no what — only a series of yours.
A broadcast can be checked afterwards. A feed cannot.

A lorry driver is parked in a lay-by at ten past midnight eating something out of a plastic tub, with the engine off and the cab light on. The radio is playing quietly because he has had it on since Peterborough. A song comes on that he has not heard before and he likes it enough to send his sister, who is four time zones away and in the middle of her afternoon, a message asking what it is called. She writes back inside a minute. She says she does not know either, but it has just started here as well.

Nothing synchronised those two people. No account was linked and no algorithm noticed a resemblance between a man in a lay-by and a woman on the other side of the world. They were on the same frequency, and the frequency was doing what a frequency does.

It has to be said plainly that the live count is a minority of the dial and will be for some time. Whole formats are silent. If your language is not among the names above, then this article, read honestly, is a list of other people’s stations. And a live station is not an indestructible one: a stream can drop, a rotation can stall, and a frequency that was playing this morning can be quiet for an hour this evening while somebody sorts it out.

But a count that can be wrong is a count that can be checked, and that is exactly why it is published as a number rather than a mood. Anybody can say they have thousands of stations. A number that goes up in ones is a number somebody has to stand behind, and it is the only kind that means anything. The same goes for the manifest and the logs: the reason to keep records that can embarrass you is that records which cannot embarrass you are not records.

So what is on air today is not a marketing figure. It is a state of affairs. A defined set of frequencies is playing defined catalogues at this moment, the tracks in them are identified permanently rather than by title, and everything else on the band is named and numbered and coming. There is nothing here you have to take on trust that could not be verified by somebody willing to sit and listen.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

Four kinds of programming sit on this dial and it helps to know they are there. Most of the band is music — praise and worship, contemporary, country, gospel, hymns and a good deal besides. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and explained and prayed through rather than sung. There is family programming, which is simply safe to have on in a room with children in it. And there are the international frequencies, hosted in their own languages rather than translated into them afterwards. No menu, no queue to assemble, and no decision to make before anything starts.

If you want somewhere to start, start at HM 308.70 — Year of Jubilee. It is the flagship of the band and it is the right test of everything above, because it is the frequency most likely to be playing when you get there and the one that will not play you the same song twice in a day. Put it on in the morning while you are doing something else. Then put it on again at the same hour tomorrow. You will land in a different place in the rotation, on a schedule you had no part in setting, exactly as you would on any transmitter that has ever existed — and that unremarkable fact is the entire claim this article has been making.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest and press play — it is built deliberately for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you would like it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else on it. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band learns which frequencies people are genuinely reaching for, which is how the next one gets built.

So take this as an invitation rather than a report. The list above will be longer at some point and there will be no announcement when it happens. Put HM 308.70 on this afternoon while you are getting on with something, and join it halfway through whatever it is playing, and do not go looking for the beginning. There is not one. That is what it means for a thing to be on the air.
